questions.q: A particle of mass 'm', moving with a velocity 'v' makes an elastic collision in one dimension with a stationary particle of mass 'm'. During the collision, they remain in contact with each other for an extremely small time 'T': Their force of contact, with time is shown in the figure. Then F0=
questions.solution:
In an elastic head-on collision between two particles, the velocity of the particle gets exchanged, therefore net change of momentum of a particle is, ∆p=m∆v=mv-0=mv

From newton's second law, the rate of change of momentum is force.

F=dpdt
⇒Fdt=dp
⇒FT=∆p

Here, F is force of contact during the collision for a small-time T that causes the ∆p change in momentum of particle.

Thus, the area under the graph of F-t curve gives the change in momentum.

Area=12×T4×F0+3T4-T4×F0+12×T-3T4×F0
=34TF0

Therefore, 

Area=∆p
⇒mv=34TF0
⇒F0=4mv3T

questions.q: A force-time $(F-t)$ graph for a linear motionis shown in following figure. The segments shown are circular. The linear momentum gained between 0 and $8 \mathrm{~s}$ is
questions.solution:
From graph, the force is varying sinusoidally with time by equation,
$F=-2 \cdot \cos \omega t$ ...(i)
where, $\omega$ be the angular frequency of variation of force.
Since, the graph is completing one cycle in $8 \mathrm{~s}$,
hence time period, $T=8 \mathrm{~s}$
Using expression of change of momentum,
$\Delta p=\int_0^8 F d t=\int_0^8-2 \cos \omega t d t$[from Eq. (i)]
$\begin{aligned} & =-\frac{2}{\omega}[\sin \omega t]_0^8 \\ & =\frac{-2}{\omega}[\sin \omega 8-\sin 0]\end{aligned}=\frac{-2}{\omega}\left[\sin \frac{2 \pi}{8} 8-0\right]\left(\because \omega=\frac{2 \pi}{T}\right)=\frac{-2}{\omega}[\sin 2 \pi]=0[\because \sin 0=\sin 2 \pi=0]$
Hence, the gain or change of linear momentum is zero.

questions.q: In figure $E$ and $v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ represent the total energy and speed of centre of mass of an object of mass $1 \mathrm{~kg}$ in pure rolling. The object is
questions.solution:
As we know, kinetic energy of an object in pure rolling motion is given as
$E=\frac{1}{2} m v_{\mathrm{cm}}^{2}\left(1+\frac{k^{2}}{R^{2}}\right)$
where, $k$ is radius of gyration and $m$ is the mass of the object.
$\Rightarrow \quad \frac{E}{v_{\mathrm{cm}}^{2}}=\frac{1}{2}\left[1+\frac{k^{2}}{R^{2}}\right] ...(i)[\because$ Given, $m=1 \mathrm{~kg}$ ]
From the given graph, substituting the value of $\frac{E}{v_{\mathrm{cm}}^{2}}$ in Eq. (i), we get
$\begin{aligned}
\frac{3}{4} &=\frac{1}{2}\left[1+\frac{k^{2}}{R^{2}}\right] \\
\Rightarrow \quad \frac{3}{2}-1 &=\frac{k^{2}}{R^{2}} \\
\Rightarrow \quad \frac{k^{2}}{R^{2}} &=\frac{1}{2}
\end{aligned}$
Since, for a
(a) Sphere, $\frac{k^{2}}{R^{2}}=\frac{2}{5}$
(b) Ring, $\frac{k^{2}}{R^{2}}=1$
(c) Hollow cylinder, $\frac{k^{2}}{R^{2}}=1$
(d) Disc, $\frac{k^{2}}{R^{2}}=\frac{1}{2}$
So, the given object is disc.

questions.q:
Assertion : Centre of mass of a system may or may not lie inside the system.
Reason : The position of centre of mass depends on distribution of mass within the system.
options: If both Assertion & Reason are true and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.
If both Assertion & Reason are true but the reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion.
If Assertion is true statement but Reason is false.
If both Assertion and Reason are false statements.
questions.solution:
- Assertion (A): True. The centre of mass (COM) can lie inside or outside the material of the body/system. Examples: for a uniform ring or a semicircular wire, the COM lies at the geometric center-which is empty space.
- Reason (R): True. The COM position is determined by the mass distribution:
\(\vec{R}_{C M}=\frac{\sum m_i \vec{r} i}{\sum m_i} \quad \text { or } \quad \vec{R} C M=\frac{1}{M} \int \vec{r} d m\)
Change how mass is spread, and the COM shifts accordingly.
- Does R explain A? Yes. Because COM depends on how mass is distributed, certain distributions (like mass arranged around a hole) naturally place the COM in a region with no material, explaining why COM may be outside the system.
Hence, both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A \(\rightarrow\) Option (1).
questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision

questions.q:
Assertion : The position of centre of mass relative to body is independent of the choice of coordinate system.
Reason : Centre of mass does not shift its position in the absence of an external force.
options: If both Assertion & Reason are true and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.
If both Assertion & Reason are true but the reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion.
If Assertion is true statement but Reason is false.
If both Assertion and Reason are false statements.
questions.solution:
Changing the coordinate system adds the same offset to all position vectors. The COM position relative to the body (i.e., measured from the body's own geometry) doesn't depend on the coordinate choice.
- Reason (R): False (as stated).
With no external force, the COM has zero acceleration, not zero motion. It can still move at constant velocity; so its position can change with time unless it happened to be at rest initially in that frame.
Therefore, A is true, R is false \(\rightarrow\) Option (3).
questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision

questions.q:
Two particles mass \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) are kept at rest at \(t=0\). They start attracting each other due to their gravitational pull, then
Statement-I: The total momentum of the system is zero at any instant.
Statement-II: Both the particles gain equal momentum in opposite direction in equal interval of time as both are acted upon equal and opposite forces.
options: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct.
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are incorrect.
Statement-I is correct and Statement-II is incorrect.
Statement-I is incorrect and Statement-II is correct.
questions.solution:
1. By Newton's third law the internal forces are equal and opposite:
\(\mathrm{F}_{12}=-\mathrm{F}_{21} .\)
If \(\mathrm{p}_1, \mathrm{p}_2\) are momenta, then
\(\frac{d \mathrm{p}_1}{d t}=\mathrm{F}_{12}, \quad \frac{d \mathrm{p}_2}{d t}=\mathrm{F}_{21}=-\mathrm{F}_{12} .\)
Add them:
\(\frac{d}{d t}\left(\mathrm{p}_1+\mathrm{p}_2\right)=0 \Rightarrow \mathrm{p}_1+\mathrm{p}_2=\text { constant }\)
Initially both particles are at rest, so \(\mathrm{p}_1+\mathrm{p}_2=\mathrm{0}\). Hence at every later time the total momentum remains zero. This proves Statement I.
2. From the pair of equations above,
\(\frac{d \mathrm{p}_1}{d t}=-\frac{d \mathrm{p}_2}{d t} .\)
Integrating over any equal time interval gives
\(\Delta \mathrm{p}_1=-\Delta \mathrm{p}_2,\)
i.e. they gain equal magnitude momenta in opposite directions (even though their velocities will be different if \(m_1 \neq m_2\)). That proves Statement II.
Both statements are therefore true (and Statement II \(\downarrow\) ist the differential form of the same Newton-third law fact that ensures Statement J).
questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision

questions.q:
Statement-I: A point particle of mass \(m\) moving with speed \(v\) collides with stationary point particle of mass \(M\). If the maximum energy loss possible is given as \(f\left(\frac{1}{2} m v^2\right)\) then \(f=\left(\frac{m}{M+m}\right)\).
Statement-II: Maximum energy loss occurs when the particles get stuck together as a result of the collision.
options: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct.
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are incorrect.
Statement-I is correct and Statement-II is incorrect.
Statement-I is incorrect and Statement-II is correct.
questions.solution:
Initial kinetic energy
\(K_i=\frac{1}{2} m v^2\)
If after collision the two masses stick (perfectly inelastic), common velocity by momentum conservation is
\(V=\frac{m v}{m+M}\)
Final kinetic energy then is
\(K_f=\frac{1}{2}(m+M) V^2=\frac{1}{2}(m+M) \frac{m^2 v^2}{(m+M)^2}=\frac{1}{2} \frac{m^2 v^2}{m+M}\)
Energy lost:
\(\Delta K=K_i-K_f=\frac{1}{2} m v^2-\frac{1}{2} \frac{m^2 v^2}{m+M}=\frac{1}{2} m v^2\left(1-\frac{m}{m+M}\right)=\frac{1}{2} m v^2 \cdot \frac{M}{m+M}\)
So the maximum fractional loss \(f\) (such that \(\Delta K=f \cdot \frac{1}{2} m v^2\)) is
\(f=\frac{M}{m+M}\)
Thus Statement-I (which asserts \(f=\frac{m}{m+M}\)) is wrong. Statement-II is correct because the maximum kinetic energy loss occurs for the perfectly inelastic case (particles stick, \(e=0\)).
questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision

questions.q:
Statement-I: Two particles moving in the same direction do not lose all their energy in a completely inelastic collision.
Statement-II: Principle of conservation of momentum holds true for all kinds of collisions.
options: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct.
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are incorrect.
Statement-I is correct and Statement-II is incorrect.
Statement-I is incorrect and Statement-II is correct.
questions.solution:
Let masses \(m_1, m_2\) have initial velocities \(u_1, u_2\) in the same direction and they stick after collision (perfectly, inelastic). Common velocity
\(v=\frac{m_1 u_1+m_2 u_2}{m_1+m_2}\)
Initial KE:
\(K_i=\frac{1}{2} m_1 u_1^2+\frac{1}{2} m_2 u_2^2,\)
Final KE:
\(K_f=\frac{1}{2}\left(m_1+m_2\right) v^2\)
Loss of kinetic energy
\(\Delta K=K_i-K_f=\frac{1}{2} \frac{m_1 m_2}{m_1+m_2}\left(u_1-u_2\right)^2 \geq 0\)
This loss is not the whole initial energy except when \(u_1=u_2\) (then \(\Delta K=0\)). So Statement-1 is true: they do not lose all their energy in general.
Statement-II is also true: momentum is conserved in all collisions provided the system is isolated (no externa impulse). That includes elastic, inelastic, perfectly inelastic collisions and explosions (internal forces only).
So both are true \(\rightarrow\) option (1).
questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision

questions.q:
Statement-I: When you lean behind over the hind legs of the chair, the chair falls back after a certain angle.
Statement-II: Centre of mass lying outside the system makes the system unstable.
options: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct.
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are incorrect.
Statement-I is correct and Statement-II is incorrect.
Statement-I is incorrect and Statement-II is correct.
questions.solution:
- Stability criterion: an object is stable as long as the vertical line through its centre of mass (CM) falls inside the base of support. If the vertical from the CM passes outside the base, the normal reaction can no longer provide a balancing moment and the object will tip.
- Apply to the chair. when you lean back on the hind legs you tilt the chair so the projection of the combined CM (you + chair) moves toward the back edge of the base. At a certain tilt angle the vertical through the CM crosses the rear edge - beyond that the CM lies outside the support polygon and the chair rotates (falls) backward. That is exactly Statement-I and it follows from Statement-II.
So both statements are true and related: the chair falls when the CM's vertical leaves the base of support.
questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision

questions.q:
Assertion (A): During collision between two objects, the momentum of colliding objects is conserved only in direction perpendicular to line of impact.
Reason (R): The force on colliding objects in perpendicular direction to line of impact is zero.
options: Assertion (A) is True, Reason (R) is True; Reason (R) is a correct explanation for Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is True, Reason (R) is True; Reason (R) is not a correct explanation for Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is True, Reason (R) is False.
Assertion (A) is False, Reason (R) is True.
questions.solution:
Assertion (A):
"During collision between two objects, the momentum of colliding objects is conserved only in direction perpendicular to line of impact."
This is false.
- In reality, linear momentum is conserved in all directions (because external force is absent).
- What is special is that along the line of impact, momentum is not separately conserved for each object (because of impulsive forces), but the total system momentum is always conserved in both perpendicular and parallel directions.
Reason (R):
"The force on colliding objects in perpendicular direction to line of impact is zero."
This is true.
- Collision forces act only along the line of impact (normal at contact).
- Therefore, perpendicular to line of impact, no impulsive force acts.
\(\checkmark\) So the correct choice is:
(4) Assertion (A) is False, Reason (R) is True.
That matches the given answer key.
questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In an elastic collision of two bodies, the momentum and energy of each body is conserved.
Reason (R): If two bodies stick to each other, after colliding, the collision is said to be perfectly inelastic.
options: Assertion (A) is True, Reason (R) is True; Reason (R) is a correct explanation for Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is True, Reason (R) is True; Reason (R) is not a correct explanation for Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is True, Reason (R) is False.
Assertion (A) is False, Reason (R) is True.
questions.solution:
- Assertion (A) is False.
- In an elastic collision, the total momentum of the system and the total kinetic energy of the system are conserved. Momentum and kinetic energy are not, in general, conserved for each body individually; they can exchange between bodies. So the phrase "of each body" makes A false.
- Reason (R) is True.
- When two bodies stick together after collision, the collision is perfectly inelastic by definition.
Therefore, the correct option is (4): Assertion (A) is False, Reason (R) is True.
questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In inelastic collision, a part of kinetic energy convert into heat energy, sound energy and light energy etc.
Reason (R): The force of interaction in an inelastic collision is non-conservative in nature.
options: Assertion (A) is True, Reason (R) is True; Reason (R) is a correct explanation for Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is True, Reason (R) is True; Reason (R) is not a correct explanation for Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is True, Reason (R) is False.
Assertion (A) is False, Reason (R) is True.
questions.solution:
- Assertion (A) is True. In an inelastic collision, total momentum is conserved but total kinetic energy of the system decreases because some of it is transformed into other forms (heat, sound, internal energy due to deformation).
- Reason (R) is True. The contact/deformation forces during an inelastic collision include non-conservative components (e.g., frictional and internal dissipative forces), so mechanical energy is not conserved.
- However, R is not the correct explanation for A in the strict assertion-reason sense: A states what happens to kinetic energy; R states a property of the forces but does not explicitly link how this causes the conversion into heat/sound/etc. Hence it's true but not a direct explanatory statement for A .
Correct option: (2) Assertion (A) is True, Reason (R) is True; Reason (R) is not a correct explanation for Assertion (A).
questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In an elastic collision between two bodies, the energy of each body is conserved.
Reason (R): The total energy of an isolated system is conserved.
options: Assertion (A) is True, Reason (R) is True; Reason (R) is a correct explanation for Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is True, Reason (R) is True; Reason (R) is not a correct explanation for Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is True, Reason (R) is False.
Assertion (A) is False, Reason (R) is True.
questions.solution:
- Assertion (A) is False. In an elastic collision, what is conserved is the total kinetic energy of the system and total momentum. The kinetic energy and momentum of each individual body generally change due to exchange during collision; they are not conserved body-by-body.
- Reason (R) is True. For an isolated system, total energy (including kinetic, potential, internal, etc.) is conserved.
Therefore, the correct option is (4): Assertion (A) is False, Reason (R) is True.

questions.q:
A body \(A\) moving with momentum \(P\) collides one-dimensionally with another stationary body \(B\) of same mass. During impact, \(A\) gives impulse \(J\) to \(B\). Then which of the following is/are correct?
(a) The total momentum of \(A\) and \(B\) is \(P\) before and after impact and \((P-J)\) during the impact.
(b) During the impact, \(B\) gives impulse of magnitude \(J\) to \(A\).
(c) The coefficient of restitution is \(\left[\frac{2 J}{P}-1\right]\).
(d) The coefficient of restitution is \(\left[\frac{2 J}{P}+1\right]\).
questions.solution:
According to the question, a collision between two bodies (\(A\) and \(B\)) is shown in the figure below,
So, the coefficient of restitution \(\begin{aligned} e & =\frac{\text { Relative velocity of separation }}{\text { Relative velocity of approach }} \\ \Rightarrow \quad e & =\frac{\frac{J-p}{m}+\frac{J}{m}}{\frac{p}{m}-0}=\frac{2 J}{P}-1 \quad\left(\because v=\frac{m v}{m}=\frac{p}{m}\right) \end{aligned}\) During the impact, \(B\) gives impulse \(J_B=p+J-p=J\) Hence, the statement (b) and (c) are correct.

questions.q:
A particle of mass m moving with a velocity \((3 \hat{\mathrm{i}}+2 \hat{\mathrm{j}}) \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}\) collides with stationary body of mass M and finally moves with velocity \((-2 \hat{\mathrm{i}}+\hat{\mathrm{j}}) \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}\) then
(A) Impulse received by \(m=m(5 \hat{i}-5 \hat{j})\)
(B) Impulse received by \(m=m(-5 \hat{i}-\hat{j})\)
(C) Impulse received by \(\mathrm{M}=\mathrm{m}(5 \hat{\mathrm{i}}+\hat{\mathrm{j}})\)
(D) Impulse received by \(M=m(5 \hat{i}-\hat{j})\) then correct statements are
questions.solution:
\(\begin{aligned}
& I=m \cdot \Delta v \\
& =m[(-2 \hat{i}+\hat{j})-(3 \hat{i}+2 \hat{j})] \\
& =m[-5 \hat{i}-\hat{j}] \rightarrow \text { Impulse on } m \\
& \text { Impulse on } M=-(\text {Impulse on } m) \\
& =m(5 \hat{i}+\hat{j})
\end{aligned}\)

questions.q:
Match the following columns with respective positions of centre of mass -
\(\begin{array}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline & \text{Column - I} & & \text{Column - II} \\
\hline \text{(A)} & \text{uniform rod length } =\mathrm{R} & \text{(P)} & \mathrm{x}=\frac{3 \mathrm{R}}{8} \\
\hline \text{(B)} & \begin{array}{l} \text{uniform thin semicircular} \\ \text{ring of radius } R \end{array} & \text{(Q)} & \mathrm{x}=\frac{\mathrm{R}}{2} \\
\hline \text{(C)} & \begin{array}{l} \text{unifiorm semicurcula} \\ \text{disc of radius } R \end{array} & \text{(R)} & \mathrm{x}=\frac{4 \mathrm{R}}{3 \pi} \\
\hline \text{(D)} & \begin{array}{l} \text{uniform solid hemisphere} \\ \text{of radius } R \end{array} & \text{(S)} & \mathrm{x}=\frac{2 \mathrm{R}}{\pi} \\
\hline
\end{array}\)
options: \(A: P, B: R, C: Q, D: S\)
\(A: Q, B: P, C: R, D: S\)
\(A: Q, B: S, C: R, D: P\)
questions.solution:
(A) Uniform rod of length \(R\)
- For a uniform rod, the COM lies exactly at the midpoint.
So, \(x=\frac{R}{2}\).
That matches (Q).
(B) Uniform thin semicircular ring of radius R
- Standard result: COM of a semicircular ring lies at a distance \(\frac{2 R}{\pi}\) from the center, along symmetry axis.
So, \(x=\frac{2 R}{\pi}\).
That matches (S).
(C) Uniform semicircular disc of radius R
- Standard result: COM of a semicircular lamina is at a distance \(\frac{4 R}{3 \pi}\) from the center along symmetry axis.
So, \(x=\frac{4 R}{3 \pi}\).
That matches (R).
(D) Uniform solid hemisphere of radius R
- Standard result: COM of a solid hemisphere is at a distance \(\frac{3 R}{8}\) from the flat face (base).
So, \(x=\frac{3 R}{8}\).
That matches (P).

questions.q:
Particle of mass m, kinetic energy K and momentum P collides head on elastically with another particle of mass 2 m at rest. After collision:
\(\begin{array}{|l|l|l|c|}
\hline & \text{Column I} & & \text{Column II} \\
\hline \text{(A)} & \text{Momentum of } \mathrm{I}^{\text {st }} \text{ particle} & \text{(P)} & \frac{4}{3} \mathrm{P} \\
\hline \text{(B)} & \text{Momentum of } \mathrm{II}^{\text {rd }} \text{ particle} & \text{(Q)} & \frac{\mathrm{K}}{9} \\
\hline \text{(C)} & \mathrm{KE}^{\text {of }} \mathrm{I}^{\text {sd }} \text{ particle} & \text{(R)} & \frac{8 \mathrm{~K}}{9} \\
\hline \text{(D)} & \mathrm{KE}^{\text {of }} \mathrm{II}^{\text {rd }} \text{ particle} & \text{(S)} & -\frac{\mathrm{P}}{3} \\
\hline
\end{array}\)
questions.solution: \(v_1 ~\&~ v_2\) are velocities after collision Conservation of linear momentum \(\begin{gathered} \mathrm{mu}=\mathrm{mv}_1+2 \mathrm{mv}_2 \\ \mathrm{u}=\mathrm{v}_1+\mathrm{v}_2 \quad \ldots (1) \\ \mathrm{e}=1=\frac{\mathrm{v}_2-\mathrm{v}_1}{\mathrm{u}} \\ \mathrm{u}=\mathrm{v}_2-\mathrm{v}_1 \quad \ldots (2) \end{gathered}\) From (1) & (2) \(v_2=\frac{2 u}{3} ; v_1=-\frac{u}{3}\) Momentum of \(1^{\text {t }}\) particle \(=-\frac{\mathrm{mu}}{3}=-\frac{\mathrm{P}}{3}\) Momentum of \(2^{\text {nd }}\) particle \(=+2 \mathrm{~m}\left(\frac{2 \mathrm{u}}{3}\right)=\frac{4 \mathrm{P}}{3}\) K.E. of \(1^a\) particle \(=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m}\left(\frac{\mathrm{u}}{3}\right)^2=\frac{\mathrm{K}}{9}\) K.E. of \(2^{\infty}\) particle \(=\frac{1}{2} \times 2 \mathrm{~m}\left(\frac{2 \mathrm{u}}{3}\right)^2=\frac{8 \mathrm{~K}}{9}\)

questions.q:
Four point masses are placed at four corners of a square of side 4 m as shown in the figure. Match the following columns.
\(\begin{array}{l|l|l|l} & \text{Column I} & & \text{Column II} \\ \hline \text { (A) } & \begin{array}{l} x \text {-coordinate of centre of mass of } \\ 4 \mathrm{~kg} \text { and } 2 \mathrm{~kg} \end{array} & \text { (p) } & (7 / 2) \mathrm{m} \\ \text { (B) } & \begin{array}{l} x \text {-coordinate of centre of mass of } \\ 4 \mathrm{~kg}, 2 \mathrm{~kg} \text { and } 3 \mathrm{~kg} \end{array} & \text { (q) } & 4 / 3 \mathrm{~m} \\ \text { (C) } & \begin{array}{l} y \text {-coordinate of centre of mass of } \\ 1 \mathrm{~kg}, 4 \mathrm{~kg} \text { and } 3 \mathrm{~kg} \end{array} & \text { (r) } & 3 \mathrm{~m} \\ \text { (D) } & \begin{array}{l} y \text {-coordinate of centre of mass of } \\ 1 \mathrm{~kg} \text { and } 3 \mathrm{~kg} \end{array} & \text { (s) } & \text { (20/9) } \mathrm{m} \\ \hline \end{array}\)
questions.solution:
Formulas:
- x-coordinate of COM: \(x=\Sigma(m i x i) / \Sigma(m i)\)
- \(y\)-coordinate of COM: \(\bar{y}=\Sigma(m \mathrm{i} \mathrm{yi}) / \Sigma(m \mathrm{i})\)
Corner coordinates used above.
A. x-coordinate of COM of 4 kg and 2 kg :
- Masses at \((0,4)\) and \((4,0) \rightarrow x^{-}=(4 \cdot 0+2 \cdot 4) /(4+2)=8 / 6=4 / 3 \mathrm{~m}\).
B. x-coordinate of COM of \(4 \mathrm{~kg}, 2 \mathrm{~kg}\), and 3 kg :
- Positions: \((0,4),(4,0),(4,4)\)
- \(x^{-}=(4 \cdot 0+2 \cdot 4+3 \cdot 4) /(4+2+3)=(0+8+12) / 9=20 / 9 \mathrm{~m}\).
C. y -coordinate of COM of \(1 \mathrm{~kg}, 4 \mathrm{~kg}\), and 3 kg :
- Positions: \((0,0),(0,4),(4,4)\)
- \(y=(1.0+4.4+3.4) /(1+4+3)=(0+16+12) / 8=28 / 8=7 / 2 \mathrm{~m}\).
D. y -coordinate of COM of 1 kg and 3 kg :
- Positions: \((0,0),(4,4)\)
- \(\bar{y}=(1.0+3.4) /(1+3)=12 / 4=3 \mathrm{~m}\).
Thus, matching to options set:
- (p) \(7 / 2 \mathrm{~m}\), (q) \(4 / 3 \mathrm{~m}\), (r) 3 m, (s) 20/9 m.

questions.q:
Match the following:
\(\begin{array}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline & \text{Column I} & & \text{Column II} \\
\hline \text { A. } & \text { Elastic collision } & \text { P. } & e=0 \\
\hline \text { B. } & \text { Inelastic collision } & \text { Q. } & O < e < 1 \\
\hline \text { C. } & \text { Explosion } & \text { R. } & e=1 \\
\hline \text { D. } & \text { Plastic collision } & \text { S. } & \text { Final K.E. }>\text { initial K.E } \\
\hline
\end{array}\)
questions.solution:
(A) Elastic collision
- By definition, perfectly elastic collision has coefficient of restitution \(e=1\).
\((A) \rightarrow(R)\).
(B) Inelastic collision
- For inelastic collisions (not perfectly plastic), coefficient of restitution lies between \(0 < e < 1\).
\(\sim(B) \rightarrow(Q)\).
(C) Explosion
- In an explosion, internal energy is released, so Final K.E. > Initial K.E.
\(\sim(C) \rightarrow(S)\).
(D) Plastic collision (perfectly inelastic)
- In a perfectly plastic collision, bodies stick together, so \(e=0\).
\(\sim(\mathrm{D}) \rightarrow(\mathrm{P})\).
